summary: Otto Karow was a scholar of Sinology, Japanology, and Tibetology who studied at Giessen, Humboldt University of Berlin, Leipzig, and Bonn. He served as a lecturer at Bonn, taught at Münster, and became professor of East Asian Philology at Frankfurt.

Otto Loth specialized in Indology and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied under Heinrich Leberecht Fleischer between circa 1866 and 1869, taught Eugen Hultzsch, and held a post at the University of Leipzig from around 1874 to 1881.

Otto Maenchen-Helfen studied Sinology, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and archaeology at Vienna, Gothenburg, and Leipzig under August Conrady. He held positions at the Marx-Engels Institute, Humboldt University of Berlin, Mills College, and the University of California, Berkeley.

Otto Rosenberg studied Buddhist studies, Japanology, and Indology at Saint Petersburg State University and the University of Bonn under Theodore Stcherbatsky, Sergey Oldenburg, Hermann Jacobi, and Rudolf Lange. He taught as a professor at Saint Petersburg State University.

Otto Schlaginhaufen earned his Ph.D. at the University of Zurich in 1905. He worked at the Rudolf-Virchow-Sammlung and the Museum of Ethnology in Dresden before serving as extraordinary and then ordinary professor of anthropology at the University of Zurich.

Otto Schrader, an Indologist and linguist, studied at Jena, Leipzig, and Humboldt University of Berlin. He worked as an Oberlehrer at Carolo-Alexandrinum Jena and held professorships of Indogermanistik at the University of Jena and the University of Breslau.

Otto Spies studied Indology and religious studies at Tübingen under Enno Littmann and at Bonn. He served as professor at Aligarh Muslim University, the University of Breslau, and the University of Bonn.

Otto Stein studied Indology and archaeology at the German University in Prague and Charles University under Moriz Winternitz and Heinrich Swoboda. He later became professor of Indology and ancient Indian culture at Charles University/the German University in Prague.

Otto Strauss studied Indology and philosophy at Munich, Berlin, and Kiel under Paul Deussen and Hermann Oldenberg. He held academic posts at Kiel University, served as professor at the University of Calcutta, and was ordinary professor at Breslau.
Otto Stursberg studied Indology and religious studies at Humboldt University of Berlin, completing his PhD around 1903-1907 under the supervision of Richard Pischel.
Otto Walter was an Indologist who studied at the University of Strasbourg from around 1899 to 1903, earning a Ph.D. under the supervision of Ernst Leumann.

Otto Wecker was an Indologist who studied at Humboldt University of Berlin, Münster, and Tübingen, where he earned his PhD under Richard von Garbe. He later taught at the University of Göttingen from 1947 to 1953.

Otto von Böhtlingk studied Indology and linguistics at Saint Petersburg, Berlin, and Bonn under Franz Bopp, Christian Lassen, and A. W. von Schlegel. He held posts at the Saint Petersburg Academy of Sciences and the University of Jena.

Otton Ottonovič Rozenberg studied Buddhist studies, Sinology, and Japanology at Saint Petersburg, Bonn, and Berlin under Fyodor Shcherbatskoy, Hermann Jacobi, and Rudolf Lange. He became a professor at Saint Petersburg State University in 1919.
Owen Flanagan is a scholar in philosophy and Buddhist studies who studied at Fordham University and Boston University. Around 1996, he was appointed Professor of Philosophy at Duke University.

Owen Lattimore, a scholar of Central Asian studies, Sinology, and history, attended St Bees School and studied at Harvard University from 1928 to 1929. He later held a post at the University of Leeds from circa 1963 to 1970.

P. A. Payutto studied Buddhist studies and philosophy at Mahachulalongkornrajavidyalaya University from circa 1956 to 1962. He served as Associate Dean there from around 1964 to 1972 and was named Tipitaka Acharaya at Nava Nalanda Mahavihara in 1995.
P. Anujan Achan studied Indology and history under Vidhushekhara Bhattacharya. He later served as Government Archaeologist at the Thrissur Zoo and State Museum.
P. B. Meegaskumbura is an Indologist, linguist, and Buddhist studies scholar who taught Naomi Appleton and was attested as a professor at the University of Peradeniya in 1991 and 2010.

P. D. Premasiri studied at Peradeniya, Cambridge, and Hawaiʻi under supervisors including David J. Kalupahana and Eliot Deutsch. A Buddhist studies and philosophy scholar, he long served as professor and department head at the University of Peradeniya.
